questions.question: What did the palm tree say about the red rose? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The palm tree **admired the beauty of the rose** and said that she wished to be **as lovely as the rose**.

**What the passage says.**

> "As the rose looked around a palm tree nearby said, 'What a beautiful floral ! I wish I was that lovely.'"

**Point to note.** The palm tree is the one friendly voice in the opening scene. It praises the rose without flattery, while the sunflower merely asks "why do you say that?" and the rose herself supplies the boasting. The palm tree's admiration is sincere but it does not save the rose from becoming vain.

questions.question: How did the red rose insult the cactus? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The rose called the cactus **ugly, a plant which has thorns only**. She said that the cactus is **useless because it does not have a pleasant colour**, and that she was sorry to be his neighbour.

**How the insult grows.** First she says, "Look at that ugly plant. It is full of thorns." Then, when the palm tree objects, she grows angrier: "this plant is useless", "how sorry I am to be his neighbour", "it does not have a pleasant colour". She even tries to move her roots away from him, but she cannot.

**Irony.** Every charge she makes — thorns, no colour, useless — turns out to be false when the cactus alone is able to give water to the thirsty birds, and the rose has to beg his help.

questions.question: How did life become difficult in the forest? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** After spring the weather became **very hot**. Life became difficult in the forest because there was **no rain for a long time**; the plants and animals needed water, the rose began to wilt and the leaves dried up and fell one by one.

**What the passage says.**

> "Spring passed and the weather became very hot. Life became difficult in the forest. There was no rain for a long time. The plants and animals needed water."

**Why it matters to the story.** The drought is the turning point. It strips the rose of the one thing she was proud of — her beauty — and reveals the worth of the plant she had despised, because the cactus stores water in its thick stem.

questions.question: How did the cactus help the birds? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The cactus **provided water to the birds**. The birds sat on its thorny branches, **stuck their beaks into the stem** and drank the water stored there, and then flew away refreshed.

**What the passage says.**

> "The birds stuck their beaks into the stem and then flew away refreshed... 'the birds got water from the cactus.'"

**Contrast.** The same thorns which the rose had mocked as "ugly" are what the birds hold on to while they drink. What she called a defect is exactly what makes the cactus useful, and that is the lesson the rose finally learns.

questions.question: What lesson did the red rose learn? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The red rose learnt that **we should never judge anyone by their appearance**.

**The lesson in context.** When the drought came, the "ugly, useless" cactus was the only plant that could help, giving water to the birds and then to the rose herself. Ashamed of her past behaviour, the rose had to ask his help, and the cactus — who "never got angry or upset" — gave it at once, saying that "God created all of us for a purpose". The rose understood two things: beauty is not the same as worth, and a good heart does not keep accounts of insults.

questions.question: Find the words from the passage which mean the same as: (i) good looking (1st para) (ii) to be of no use (4th para).
questions.answer:
**Answer.** (i) good looking — **beautiful**; (ii) to be of no use — **useless**.

**As used in the passage.**

> "What a **beautiful** floral ! I wish I was that lovely." (1st para)

> "...this plant is **useless**", "how sorry I am to be his neighbour" (4th para)

**How to score.** Write only the two words; do not explain them, and do not write "beauty" for (i), because the paper asks for the adjective that means *good looking*.

questions.question: Read the passage on the carbon cycle and find seven important points in it; make notes using sub-headings and headings, and give a suitable title.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Title: Carbon — The Element of Life**

1. **Carbon in living things**
   (a) main element in living beings
   (b) found in the tissues and organs of the body
   (c) present in plants, animals and in carbon dioxide

2. **Carbon dioxide in nature**
   (a) animals breathe it out
   (b) plants take it in
   (c) plant & animal waste decomposed by bacteria, which release CO₂

3. **Fossil fuels**
   (a) formed from tiny sea creatures, plants that died millions of yrs ago
   (b) oil, natural gas & coal
   (c) contain large amounts of "locked up" carbon

4. **Burning of fuels**
   (a) carbon atoms released into the air as CO₂
   (b) atoms used over & over again

5. **The carbon cycle**
   (a) atmosphere → plants → animals → atmosphere
   (b) an example of natural recycling

6. **Human activity upsets the balance**
   (a) burning fossil fuels adds more CO₂ than plants can remove
   (b) recycling of materials reduces the harm

7. **The greenhouse effect**
   (a) CO₂ works like the glass of a greenhouse
   (b) lets sunlight in, traps heat
   (c) without it the earth would be colder
   (d) excess CO₂ → global warming / greenhouse effect

**Key to abbreviations.** CO₂ – carbon dioxide; atmos. – atmosphere; temp. – temperature; g.h. – greenhouse; recycl. – recycling.

questions.question: Write a summary of the carbon-cycle passage in about 80 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Carbon is the main element of life. It is present in every unit of the body, in all living things, and in the carbon dioxide that animals breathe out and plants take in. Fossil fuels — oil, gas and coal — contain large amounts of carbon locked up from creatures that died millions of years ago, and burning them releases that carbon into the air. Carbon atoms then pass from the atmosphere to plants, to animals and back. This is the carbon cycle, an example of natural recycling. Human activity is upsetting the balance and increasing global warming.

**Word count.** About 95 words. Keep the order of the passage — element, carbon dioxide, fossil fuels, cycle, imbalance — so that the examiner can tick the points in sequence.

questions.question: You have lost your I.D. card in your school/college campus. Write a notice for the notice board in about 50 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**KENDRIYA VIDYALAYA, RANCHI**

**NOTICE**

*20th Feb, 2016*

**LOST I.D. CARD**

During the lunch break I lost my school I.D. card in the school campus. The finder is requested to return the same to the undersigned. A treat is promised.

**Manju Verma**
XII-B
Roll No. 101

**Format points.** The word NOTICE, the name of the institution, the date, what was lost, where, and what the finder should do, then the writer's name and class; keep it within 50 words and put it inside a box.

questions.question: You have an old mobile phone in good condition which you want to sell. Write an advertisement to be published in a newspaper.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**FOR SALE**

A brand new **'Microsoft Lumia - 950'** is available for sale. It is hardly used for two months. It has **1 GB RAM, 1 GHz Dual core processor, expandable memory up to 32 GB** and a **rear camera of 8 MP** with a **front camera of 3.2 MP**. It is still in the warranty period. Price **negotiable up to 5000/-**. Interested people can ring **9835197332**.

**Format points.** A classified advertisement is written in a single paragraph under a heading in block capitals, gives the quality, the specification, the price and the contact number, and — in a newspaper — is charged by the line, so no address or salutation is needed.

questions.question: You attended your cousin's wedding recently. Describe the events which took place there in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**COUSIN'S WEDDING**

Last Tuesday I attended one of my cousin's marriage ceremonies at her place. It was done with great pomp and show. Great preparations were made a month before. The whole house was decorated and many purchases were done. All the relatives were gathered.

The marriage party arrived at 7 p.m. The guests were welcomed with garlands, and an elder sister offered a token of love by applying *tilak* to the bridegroom. The bridegroom came riding on a mare, dressed in a cream sherwani and a pink turban, with the band playing in front. The guests were served dinner — puri, kachori, three kinds of vegetables and kheer — and they left the place after dinner.

The bridegroom and his relatives stayed for the holy ceremony. It was done by the pandit after midnight, and the *vidaai* took place early next morning. The parting scene was very heart-touching: my aunt wept and my cousin kept looking back at the gate.

**Word count.** About 150 words; trim the menu if a strict 125 is demanded.

questions.question: Your college/school celebrated the Republic Day with songs and a cultural event. Write a report to be published in the school/college magazine.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**REPUBLIC DAY CELEBRATION**

*Staff Reporter*

**Ranchi, 26 January 2016.** We celebrated Republic Day with great pomp and show in our school campus. Our Principal, along with the school staff and students, attended the function.

The programme began at 8 a.m. with the **hoisting of the National Flag** by the Principal, followed by the **National Anthem**. The students then did a **march past to salute the national flag**, house by house, in their white uniforms. Students sang patriotic songs and presented a cultural event — a skit on the making of the Constitution, a group dance on folk tunes and a recitation of "Where the Mind is Without Fear".

In his address the Principal reminded us of the duties that come with our rights and gave away prizes to the winners of the essay competition. Sweets were distributed to all. It was a grand occasion and the whole campus echoed with the cry of *Jai Hind*.

**Format points.** A report has a headline, the reporter's byline, the place and date, and the events in the order in which they happened, written in the **past tense and the third person**.

questions.question: You wish to do B.A./B.Sc./B.Com. from St. Stephen's College, Ranchi. Write a letter to the Principal asking for information regarding admission in the college in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Pappu Pandey**
ABC Colony, Pandra
20 February 2016

The Principal
St. Stephen's College
Ranchi

**Subject: Asking for information related to admission**

Sir

With due request I want to say that I have just passed my 12th examination with **89% marks** and I want to take admission in your college in **B.Sc.**

I request you to please provide me proper information regarding admission in your college — the last date for submission of the form, the fee for the first year, the subjects offered in the science stream, whether admission is made on the basis of the Board result or through an entrance test, and the documents required at the time of admission. I shall be grateful to you for this great help.

I shall call at your office next week for a prospectus if it is available.

Yours faithfully
**Pappu Pandey**

**Format points.** A letter of enquiry states the writer's qualification and the course wanted, then asks **specific** questions in a numbered or linked form; vague requests lose marks.

questions.question: Write a letter to the Editor of *The Hindustan Times*, Ranchi, expressing your concern about deforestation in Jharkhand in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**3, Model Town**
**Dhanbad**
**February 18, 2016**

The Editor
*The Hindustan Times*
Ranchi

**Subject: Concern about deforestation in Jharkhand**

Sir

Through the columns of your esteemed paper I want to draw the attention of the concerned authorities towards the effect of deforestation in Jharkhand. Trees are cut rapidly to fulfil our requirement. Actually forests are the pride of Jharkhand, but now we are losing it. It results in increase in temperature, uneven climate and less rainfall.

As forest is the lungs of our place, deforestation is one of the biggest causes of all types of pollution. Thousands of trees are felled every year for timber, for charcoal and for the expansion of towns, and no one plants in their place. If this continues, the coming generation will know Jharkhand's sal forests only from photographs.

I hope people will understand and think about it, and that the department will act before it is too late.

Yours faithfully
**Pappu**

**Format points.** State the problem, give its consequences, suggest the remedy — "afforestation, strict laws and public awareness" — and close formally.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Global Warming'.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**GLOBAL WARMING**

Rise in the temperature of the earth is called **Global Warming**. In today's modern age we are cutting trees rapidly. Trees maintained the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the environment. As the number of trees is decreasing, the atmosphere is becoming unbalanced.

Some gases such as **carbon dioxide, argon, nitrous oxide** etc. absorb the sun's heat and make the earth's surface hotter. They are essential for us, but only in a limited amount. As these greenhouse gases are increasing, the global temperature is also rising. Due to global warming the **glaciers are melting**. If all the glaciers melt, the whole earth will be sunk — the seas will rise and swallow the coastal cities and the fertile deltas.

It is really a major problem for us. We must plant trees, reduce the use of fossil fuels and shift to solar and wind energy. Governments may sign treaties, but the earth is cooled or warmed by the daily habits of ordinary people.

**Format points.** Title, writer's name below the title, three or four paragraphs moving from cause to consequence to remedy, and a firm conclusion.

questions.question: India is recognised as a modern 21st century economy, yet many communities continue to marry children at a very young age. Write an article on the topic 'Child Marriage'.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**CHILD MARRIAGE — A BLOT ON MODERN INDIA**

India today sends rockets to Mars and builds software for the whole world, and yet in many districts a girl is still married off before she has finished school. This contradiction is the shame of our "modern" century.

Child marriage destroys a girl's childhood. She is taken out of school, given the burden of a household and often of motherhood while her own body is still growing. Early pregnancy brings anaemia, weak children and, all too often, death in childbirth. The boy is no better prepared; he is expected to earn for a family when he should be learning a trade.

The law is clear — the **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006** makes the marriage of a girl below eighteen and a boy below twenty-one a punishable offence. But laws do not reach the village where the panchayat decides, or the family that believes it is protecting its honour by "settling" a daughter early.

The remedy must begin with **education, awareness and economic security**. Keep girls in school, give their mothers work, and let the village officer and the police act without fear. Only then will the twenty-first century economy become a twenty-first century society.

**Format points.** A provocative title, a fact or two, causes, consequences, the legal position and a remedy — this is the standard structure for a social-issue article.

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet of the extract: '... I saw my mother beside me, / doze, open mouthed, her face ashen like that / of a corpse and realised with pain / that she was as old as she looked but soon / put that thought away, and looked out ...'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **My Mother at Sixty-Six**; poet — **Kamala Das**.

**Context.** The lines occur early in the poem, as the poet sits beside her mother in a car on the way to the airport at Cochin. Her mother is dozing, "open mouthed", her face "ashen like that of a corpse", and the daughter realises "with pain" that her mother is as old as she looks. That thought is unbearable, so she "put that thought away" and looked out of the window at young trees and merry children.

questions.question: What did the poet realise and why was she sad? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet realised that **her mother was so old**, her face "ashen like that of a corpse" and "as old as she looked". She was sad **on realising the approach of death** and the coming separation from her mother.

**Explanation.** The sadness is the old childhood fear returning: as a girl she dreaded the thought of losing her mother, and now the visible decay of age brings that fear back. Kamala Das writes that she felt "the old familiar ache", the same pain she had known as a child, and she can only mask it with a smile.

questions.question: Why did the poet look out? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet looked out **because she did not want to see the pain on her mother's face**. The sight of the ageing mother made her think of death and separation, so she looked at the "young trees" and "merry children" outside.

**Explanation.** The contrast is deliberate: the sprinting trees and playing children stand for life and youth, the sleeping mother for age and death. Looking out is an escape from a truth she cannot change, and it prepares the reader for the false cheer of the last line — "see you soon, amma" / "all I say is, see you soon, amma".

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet of the extract: 'Far from the gusty waves these children's faces / Like rootless weeds, their hair torn round their pallor; / The tall girl with her weighed-down head.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum**; poet — **Stephen Spender**.

**Context.** These lines open the description of the slum classroom in Spender's poem: the children's faces are "like rootless weeds", their hair "torn round their pallor", and a tall girl sits with a "weighed-down head". The images insist that these children are starved, neglected and without any root in a secure world.

**Syllabus note.** This chapter is **outside the current syllabus** (deleted text), but the extract still appears in older question banks, so it is kept here for reference.

questions.question: Whom does the poet call 'rootless weeds'? Why? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet calls the **faces of the children of the slum areas** "rootless weeds". He does so because they are **pale, weak and neglected**, growing unwanted like weeds, with no home, care or future.

**Explanation.** A weed grows without being planted or tended, in any crack where it can find space, and it is pulled up without regret. The simile says that these children have the same insecure, unwanted existence: their hair is "torn round their pallor" and they have "spectacles of steel" with "mended glass". Later in the poem Spender contrasts them with the map on the wall, whose "lead sky" and "sun" they will never reach.

questions.question: How does the poet describe the tall girl? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The tall girl was looking **pale**. Due to the burden, **her head was weighed down**. She sits with her head drooping, exhausted, as though the weight of poverty and hunger pressed on her neck.

**Explanation.** The single detail — a lowered head — tells the whole condition of the class. Spender uses it with the "paper-seeming boy", the "rootless weeds" and the children "sores on their body" to show malnutrition and despair before he ever mentions the slum itself.

questions.question: What was the poet's childhood fear? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet's childhood fear was the **fear of old age, decay and ultimate death** — and, more personally, the fear of losing her mother.

**Explanation.** In "My Mother at Sixty-Six" Kamala Das says that looking at her ageing mother she felt "the old familiar ache", her childhood's fear. As a child she was afraid that her mother would grow old and die and leave her; as an adult she finds the same fear returning, now with reason. The poem's famous last line, "all I say is, see you soon, amma", is a smile put on to hide exactly that fear.

questions.question: Why does Pablo Neruda want us to keep quiet? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet Pablo Neruda is of the opinion that **most of our ills and troubles stem from the rush and hurry of our actions**. He urges us **not to do anything in haste** without considering all aspects of our actions and their consequences.

**Explanation.** He asks us to count to twelve and "keep still", because in that stillness "we would all be together in a sudden strangeness". The silence would stop the fisherman harming the whale, make the salt-gatherer look at his hurt hands and stop those who "prepare for war". Before doing anything we should, in his words, do "some introspection and soul-searching" — the pause is not idleness but a chance to understand ourselves.

questions.question: According to Keats, beauty will never pass into nothingness. How? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** John Keats, a great humanist and romantic poet, was a worshipper of the beautiful things of nature. He makes it clear that **a thing of beauty is a source of joy and happiness**; its charm never diminishes but goes on increasing with time.

**Explanation.** In "A Thing of Beauty" beauty is "a joy for ever" whose loveliness "increases; it will never / pass into nothingness". Keats offers examples — the sun, the moon, the trees, the daffodils, the clear rills and the musk-rose blooms — and says their "mighty fountain" keeps "a bower quiet for us" and gives us "sleep full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing". Beauty therefore outlives the moment in which it is seen.

questions.question: Describe Aunt Jennifer's fingers. (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Aunt Jennifer's hands are **moving through her wool** as she is weaving tigers on the panel. **Her fingers are fluttering**, and they are so weak that she can **pull even the ivory needle only with difficulty**.

**Explanation.** Adrienne Rich writes that "Aunt Jennifer's finger fluttering through her wool / Find even the ivory needle hard to pull". The word "fluttering" suggests nervous, uncertain movement, and the difficulty with the needle shows how the wedding ring — "the massive weight of Uncle's wedding band" — sits heavy on her hand. The weakness of the fingers is the poem's physical image of a woman mastered by her husband.

questions.question: Why was M. Hamel wearing his best dress? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** It was his **last class**. So M. Hamel wanted to teach everything that he knew. It was a **special day** for him; therefore he dressed in his best clothes — his beautiful green coat, frilled shirt and little black embroidered silk cap.

**Explanation.** In "The Last Lesson" the order has come from Berlin that only German will be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine, so this is the final French lesson. The dress marks the solemnity of the occasion, and Franz, arriving late and fearing a scolding, is instead astonished by it.

questions.question: Who was Saheb? What did he do to earn money? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Saheb was a **young boy** who left his home long ago in the **green fields of Dhaka**. He was a **ragpicker**; he scrounged for gold in the garbage dumps of Seemapuri.

**Explanation.** In "Lost Spring" Saheb-e-Alam — whose name means "lord of the universe" — walks barefoot through the streets of the city, hoping to find "a rupee, or ten-rupee note" in the garbage. He later takes work at a tea-stall for eight hundred rupees and all his meals, and the author notes that though the job pays, it costs him his freedom: he is no longer his own master.

questions.question: How did the old crofter earn thirty kronor? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The old crofter had a **cow** that gave milk for the creamery every day. By selling this milk, he earned thirty kronor.

**Explanation.** In "The Rattrap" the old man, once a crofter on the Ramsjö estate, lives alone with his cow after his sons left and his wife died. He tells the peddler proudly that the creamery paid him thirty kronor the previous month, and shows him the three ten-kronor notes stuffed in a leather pouch. The peddler watches him hide the money, and steals it the next morning — the act that leads him into the forest and into Edla's care.

questions.question: Why was Gandhiji not allowed to draw water from Rajendra Prasad's well at Patna? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The servants of Rajendra Prasad took Gandhi for an **untouchable**. In those days untouchables were **not allowed to draw water** from the well belonging to upper castes, because a drop from their bucket would pollute the entire source.

**Explanation.** In "Indigo" Gandhi stays at the house of Rajendra Prasad, and the servants, not knowing who he is, refuse to let him draw water. The episode is quietly ironic: the man who has come to fight the sharecroppers' bondage in Champaran is himself treated as an outcaste in the house of a future President of India, and neither the hosts nor the guest makes an issue of it — Gandhi simply waits to be served.

questions.question: Who were Sophie and Jansie? What were the differences between them? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Sophie and Jansie were **classmates and friends**. There were some stark differences between them: **Sophie was a dreamer while Jansie was a practical girl**. After her schooling Sophie wanted to go to a **boutique**.

**Explanation.** Jansie was doubtful about the plan because it required money, which Sophie did not have. She told Sophie it would take her a long time to save so much; Sophie said she would be a manager, and Jansie retorted that they would not make her manager straight off. Sophie dreamt of being an actress or a fashion designer, and of meeting **Danny Casey**; Jansie had no such fancies, and she warned Sophie that her story would spread through the neighbourhood. Sophie, in fact, suspected that Geoff — her brother — had told Jansie about her feelings for Danny Casey.

questions.question: Why do most celebrity writers dislike being interviewed? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Since its invention a little over 130 years ago, the interview has become a **commonplace of journalism**, read by almost everybody. **Several thousand celebrities have been interviewed over the years, some of them repeatedly**, so it is hardly surprising that their opinion of the interview varies considerably — and mostly for the worse.

**Explanation.** From Christopher Silvester's "The Interview", taken from *The Penguin Book of Interviews*: many writers feel the interview wounds them, because a careless remark is printed as a considered opinion, and the interviewer, not the author, controls what the reader sees. H. G. Wells called interviewing "an affront", and Rudyard Kipling said it was "immoral" and "a crime" — the chapter's examples of the dislike.

questions.question: Write the story 'The Last Lesson' in your own words. (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** There was an unusual atmosphere in school at Alsace on its last day. There was no bustle, it was all so still, there was no commotion. That day everything was as quiet as Sunday morning. **M. Hamel was dressed in his best**. Village people were sitting quietly at the back of the room; they had come to thank M. Hamel for his forty years' service to the school and to pay their respect to the country that was not their own any more.

M. Hamel was heart-broken. Everything looked grave and solemn. M. Hamel was very serious in teaching his lessons and the students were very attentive in learning. A new love had dawned in them for their language. Every object of the school was moving in the eyes of M. Hamel, where he had spent forty years of his life. He was sad at heart that he was leaving his school; he was hearing his sister moving about in the room above, packing their trunks. When the church clock struck twelve, M. Hamel stood up, very pale, in his chair. He dismissed the school and asked the students they might go.

**The point of the story.** Franz, who had come to school dreading his grammar lesson, discovers that the lesson he has been avoiding is the last one he will ever get in his own language. The order from Berlin has made the French language a thing to be loved, and the value of a thing is understood only when it is taken away.

questions.question: What happened to William Douglas at the YMCA swimming pool when he was eleven years old? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** When William Douglas was ten or eleven years old he decided to learn to swim. There was a pool at the Y.M.C.A. in Yakima that offered the opportunity; the Yakima River was treacherous and his mother had warned him against it, but the pool was safe.

Douglas got a pair of water wings and went to the pool. He hated to walk naked into it and show his skinny legs, but he subdued his pride and did it. From the beginning he had an aversion to the water when he was in it — an aversion that had started when he was three or four and a wave at a California beach knocked him down and "buried" him.

His introduction to the pool revived those unpleasant memories. But after a while he gathered confidence. He paddled with his new water wings, watching the other boys and trying to learn by aping them. He did this two or three times on different days and was just beginning to feel at ease when the misadventure happened: a big boy of eighteen picked him up and tossed him into the deep end. He went straight to the bottom, came up with his lungs aching, and sank again; the fear he had carried from the beach became a terror that stayed with him for years.

questions.question: How did Dr. Sadao Hoki help the American soldier? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Dr. Sadao peered into the white man's wound with the bright surgeon's light fastened on his forehead. The bullet was still there. The patient was bleeding profusely; he had lost much blood. However, Dr. Sadao continued his efforts. Then he felt the tip of his instrument strike against something hard, dangerously near the kidney. But his skilled fingers worked wonders. He made a clean and precise incision. The bullet was out in a few minutes. He gave him an injection and the white man's pulse grew stronger. Thus Sadao succeeded in saving the life of the wounded prisoner of war.

**What it cost him.** The operation was the easy part. Keeping the man hidden in his house, with the servants refusing to enter the room and the police and the army searching for the escaped prisoner, put Sadao and Hana in danger of arrest for harbouring an enemy. The doctor's decision — to treat the man as a patient rather than as a prisoner — is the moral centre of the story.

questions.question: How did Charley reach the third level of the Grand Central Station? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The corridor Charley was in began angling left and slanting downward. He kept on walking. All he could hear was the empty sound of his own footsteps, and he didn't pass a soul. Then he heard that sort of hollow roar ahead that means open space and people talking. The tunnel turned sharp left. He went down a short flight of stairs and came out on the **third level** at Grand Central Station.

**Why it was strange.** The Grand Central that Charley knows has only two levels; the third one should not exist. Yet he found himself on a platform lit by old gas lamps, with a locomotive of a kind that had stopped running fifty years earlier and a newsboy shouting about a war with Germany. He bought two tickets to Galesburg, Illinois — a town of his boyhood — before he ran out of money and had to return. The third level, in Jack Finney's story, is the past he cannot quite re-enter.

questions.question: What did the astrologer say when the Tiger King was born? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The astrologer predicted that one day the boy would have to die, and that **death would come from the tiger**. The **hundredth tiger** would be the cause of his death.

**Explanation.** In Kalki's story the chief astrologer reads the horoscope of the infant prince and warns that he will meet his end through a tiger. The Maharaja spends his life killing tigers to defeat the prophecy. Irony follows irony: the hundredth tiger is a wooden toy bought from a shop for his son's birthday, and a tiny sliver from it kills him — and the prophecy is fulfilled to the letter.

questions.question: Where did Charley want to go? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Charley wanted to go to **Galesburg, Illinois** — the town of his boyhood. He decided to take the subway from Grand Central, but he reached the **third level**.

**Explanation.** On the third level of Grand Central he bought two tickets to Galesburg for himself and his wife Louisa, because the Galesburg he saw there was "a wonderful town still, with big old frame houses, huge lawns, and tremendous trees". He wanted, in other words, to go back to the "peaceful and quiet" world of 1894 that he had never actually known.

questions.question: Why did Bama laugh when she saw the elder? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** One day Bama saw an elder coming from the market. He was carrying a **small packet by its string without touching it**, and he **gave it to the landlord**. On seeing this incident, Bama laughed.

**Explanation.** As a child, in "Memories of Childhood" by Bama, the sight of an old man carrying a packet by its string, holding it far from himself, seemed comic — the string looked as if it were a leash. Only later did her brother Annam explain that the man was a "lower-caste" person who was not allowed to touch the packet because the upper-caste shopkeeper did not want to be polluted by his touch. Bama's laughter turned to shame and anger.

questions.question: Why was Zitkala-Sa uncomfortable? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Zitkala-Sa reached the dining hall for the first time. She **knew little about the table manner to suit that place**. A small bell was sounded, and each one drew a chair from under the table; she also pulled her chair out and sat on it, though she was the only one seated.

**Explanation.** In her account, everyone else remained standing, and a pale-faced woman watched her keenly; the second bell also found them standing. She felt shy and out of place, and when the third bell rang and the others picked up their knives and forks she began crying instead of eating — a small breach of custom that grew out of her ignorance of the school's ways.

questions.question: Why were special arrangements made by the Examination Board inside the prison? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** "Wily and crafty" Evans was called **'Evans the Breaker'** by the prison staff. He had already **escaped three times** from the prison, throwing dust in the eyes of the staff. This time the authorities did not want to give any chance to Evans to escape.

**Explanation.** From "Evans Tries an O-Level" (a chapter now outside the current syllabus): because Evans was to sit an O-Level examination in his own cell, the Governor of the prison, who was particularly apprehensive about him, decided to look after all the security arrangements himself — the examination room was searched, a guard was posted, and the papers were checked by the Examination Board. All the precautions were in vain, since Evans escaped disguised as the invigilator.
